 , width=377 ]    future wl surveys will certainly put more stringent constraints on cosmological parameters and will be crucial to break quite a few degeneracies between parameters .    within this context , in this paper 
 we focus on coupled de models with a twofold aim . 
 detecting a signal of dm  de coupling would be certainly decisive to fix the nature of the dark components . henceforth determining the level of sensitivity needed to appreciate such an effect is crucial in setting the appeal of forthcoming projects . 
 there is however a complementary aspect which deserves much attention . in order to convert raw data into physical information , 
 a set of parameters , spanning a variety of models , is to be fixed ; a bias on parameter selection , however , can lead to an optimistic estimate of the confidence level for the best fitting model , far from reality .    in this paper , we focused on this kind of danger , when we open the option of dm  de coupling . 
 even if such coupling is absent or quite weak , we showed that just considering its possibility may widen the error bars for a number of parameters , also apparently unrelated to the coupling itself . in a sense , 
 when a new degree of freedom is opened , such an effect is natural and expected . 
 coupling , however , has really a major impact , affecting different parameters for the different observables considered here ; moreover , its impact is drastically reduced when we work out parameter values by using simultaneously both observables .    before outlining our main conclusions it is however worth reminding a technical limit we had to face . 
 while cmb predictions depend on linear spectra , the wl spectrum is limited to its non  linear shape . 
 for the purpose of the present analysis , we assumed that prescription for @xmath3cdm models @xcite can be trivially extrapolated to coupled models , so enabling us to estimate the non linear spectrum once the linear spectrum is known .

Generate two (2) distinct **Task Requirements**. These documents act as "System Prompts" that enable an AI to perform high-value operations on the dataset, meticulously calibrated to the persona's constraints.

**Logic Dimensions for Task Synthesis:**
* **Reasoning Depth:** Integrate industry-specific frameworks (e.g., SWOT, First Principles, Regulatory Compliance).
* **Persona-Centric Transformation:** Convert raw data fields into narrative-driven or decision-ready formats.
* **Column Selection:** Do not feel obligated to use the entire schema. Focus on the most impactful columns for the specific use case.
* **Complexity Split:** * * **Task A (Medium):** Requires interpretive reasoning. The AI must move beyond surface-level summarization to infer intent, identify conflicting data points, or predict a singular outcome. It requires the AI to apply the persona’s "expert lens" to prioritize which data columns truly matter for a specific decision.
    * **Task B (High):** Requires multi-dimensional synthesis and adversarial reasoning. The AI must cross-reference disparate data sources to resolve systemic contradictions, simulate secondary effects of specific decisions, and formulate a high-stakes strategy. 

**Each Task Requirement must include:**

    "abstract":"we study analytic surfaces in 3-dimensional euclidean space containing two circular arcs through each point . 
 the problem of finding such surfaces traces back to the works of darboux from xixth century . 
 we reduce finding all such surfaces to the algebraic problem of finding all pythagorean 6-tuples of polynomials . 
 the reduction is based on the schicho parametrization of surfaces containing two conics through each point and a new approach using quaternionic rational parametrization .    * keywords * : darboux cyclide , circle , moebius geometry , quaternion , pythagorean n - tuple    * 2010 msc * : 51b10 , 14j26 , 16h05"

    "article":"a cluster category is a certain 2-calabi - yau orbit category of the derived category of a hereditary abelian category . 
 cluster categories were introduced in @xcite in order to give a categorical model for the combinatorics of fomin - zelevinsky cluster algebras @xcite . 
 they are triangulated @xcite and admit ( cluster-)tilting objects , which model the clusters of a corresponding ( acyclic ) cluster algebra @xcite . each cluster in a fixed cluster algebra comes together with a finite quiver , and in the categorical model this quiver is in fact the gabriel quiver of the corresponding tilting object @xcite . 
 a principal ingredient in the construction of a cluster algebra is quiver mutation . 
 it controls the exchange procedure which gives a rule for producing a new cluster variable and hence a new cluster from a given cluster . 
 exchange is modeled by cluster categories in the acyclic case @xcite in terms of a mutation rule for tilting objects , i.e. a rule for replacing an indecomposable direct summand in a tilting object with another indecomposable rigid object , to get a new tilting object . 
 quiver mutation describes the relation between the gabriel quivers of the corresponding tilting objects . 
 analogously to the definition of the cluster category , for a positive integer @xmath0 , it is natural to define a certain @xmath1-calabi - yau orbit category of the derived category of a hereditary abelian category .

 @xmath0-cluster category_. implicitly , @xmath0-cluster categories was first studied in @xcite , and their ( cluster-)tilting objects have been studied in @xcite . 
 combinatorial descriptions of @xmath0-cluster categories in dynkin type @xmath2 and @xmath3 are given in @xcite .    in cluster categories 
 the mutation rule for tilting objects is described in terms of certain triangles called _ exchange triangles_. by @xcite the existence of exchange triangles generalizes to @xmath0-cluster categories . 
 it was shown in @xcite that there are exactly @xmath1 non - isomorphic complements to an almost complete tilting object , and that they are determined by the @xmath1 exchange triangles defined in @xcite . 
 the aim of this paper is to give a combinatorial description of mutation in @xmath0-cluster categories . _ a priori _ 
 , one might expect to be able to do this by keeping track of the gabriel quivers of the tilting objects . 
 however , it is easy to see that the gabriel quivers do not contain enough information .    we proceed to associate to a tilting object a quiver each of whose arrows has an associated colour @xmath4 . the arrows with colour 0 form the gabriel quiver of the tilting object . 
 we then define a mutation operation on coloured quivers and show that it is compatible with mutation of tilting objects . 
 a consequence is that the effect of an arbitrary sequence of mutations on a tilting object in an @xmath0-cluster category can be calculated by a purely combinatorial procedure . 
 our definition of a coloured quiver associated to a tilting object makes sense in any @xmath1-calabi - yau category , such as for example those studied in @xcite .

    "article":"recently , interests have been generated on cooling techniques for mechanical systems at nano- and micron - scales @xcite . among them , 
 the typically employed is the feedback cooling technique where an external feedback circuit is responsible for detecting the motion of the target and feeding a counteracting force against this motion ; through a general decrease of magnitude in the density noise spectrum , it was shown that the feedback can effectively reduce the fluctuation of the target and provide a cooling mechanism @xcite . 
 some experiments based on the models that contain the feedback loops have been carried out in the past few years . 
 a few are directed towards the cooling of micron- to nanometer - size mechanical resonators , aiming to reach a macroscopic quantum mechanical ground state and serving as a powerful manifestation of quantum mechanical effects @xcite . 
 other experiments succeed in slowing down the motion of micron - size mirrors through the radiation pressure of an optical field in a fabry - prot ( fp ) cavity , aiming to reach a noise level and equivalently an effective temperature that are pertinent to the employment of high - precision detection of gravity waves @xcite . 
 the forementioned implementations of feedback cooling through reduction of noise fluctuations invariably rely on an electrical circuitry external to the target system to be cooled . 
 the controller here is usually fixed and attracts or repels the resonator through either electrostatic coulomb force or lorentzian force . 
 if such an external detection - control unit could be eliminated in favor of a mechanism with self - detection of and self - adjustment to the target s thermal motion , we call the mechanism `` self - cooling '' @xcite . devices implementing this self - cooling use less components and are free from the reliance on an external circuitry and hence prone to less noise sources .    in one case @xcite , an augmented cavity along with an extra optical cavity field is established on the other side of the mirror , in addition to the regular fp cavity , so as to counteract the radiation pressure from the original cavity field . 
 this extra field cushions the motion of the pressure mirror and plays the role of feedback . in another case 
 @xcite , a set of josephson junctions behaving as a qubit , serially connected to a mechanical resonating beam , serves delayed supercurrent into the circuit according to the magnetic flux through the circuit loop . 
 the magnetic flux is controlled by the vibrating motion of the beam , which in turn is controlled by the magnetic field generated by the current feed . 
 such a mutual dependence furnishes a self - feedback mechanism . 
 it should be pointed out that both of the self - feedback setups require delayed feedback , which assumed _ a priori _ a non - markovian approximation that explicitly depends on the history of the target s motion . in these phenomenological treatments , the cooling target either couples itself to a static controller and makes itself prone to the noise stemmed from the feedback , or couples to a mechanically static detection construct and receives manually delayed feedback .    hereby , we present a dynamic model based on an intrinsic mechanism with non - markovian feedback , which is obviously free from an external feedback loop and does not rely on a presupposition of historical dependence . 
 this mechanism is illustrated by a simple mechanical system in which the target is modeled by a harmonic oscillator and attached to a dynamic controller , which is a relatively heavier resonator , through a spring . 
 the target is controlled by an intrinsic feedback through the dynamics of coupling : earlier positions and velocities of the target affects the motion of the controller and this influence is subsequently fed back to the target . 
 consequently , the accumulation of earlier states of the target will affect the state of itself later . with proper parameter setup 
 , the target essentially experiences a resistance and decelerates its motion ; its displacement variance is shrunk , noise suppressed and effective temperature cooled down . the lack of a specific detection device for the motion of the target resonator and an external feedback circuit characterizes the intrinsic nature of the mechanical feedback . 
 our numerical analysis shows the existence of a noise suppression capability of our scheme , e.g. the variance of displacement can be reduced to @xmath0 , and therefrom a cooling capability under a practical setting accessible in current experiments . 
 we note that the scheme is theoretically illustrative through its simple model setup yet widely applicable because the general oscillator systems can be extended to quantum bosonic systems and other cases . 
 in fact , a similar model and mechanism has been proposed to actively cool down the torsional vibration of a nanomechanical resonator through spin - orbit interactions @xcite .

 the complete solution of the system dynamics is given in sec.[sec : exact_soln ] , with which we will derive the density noise spectrum and calculate the theoretical noise suppression rate . 
 the associated numerical results will be presented in sec.[sec : num_analysis ] , given various parameter setups .

## Objective 1: High-Fidelity Task Generation
Generate two (2) distinct **Task Requirements**. These documents act as "System Prompts" that enable an AI to perform high-value operations on the dataset, meticulously calibrated to the persona's constraints.

**Logic Dimensions for Task Synthesis:**
* **Reasoning Depth:** Integrate industry-specific frameworks (e.g., SWOT, First Principles, Regulatory Compliance).
* **Persona-Centric Transformation:** Convert raw data fields into narrative-driven or decision-ready formats.
* **Column Selection:** Do not feel obligated to use the entire schema. Focus on the most impactful columns for the specific use case.
* **Complexity Split:** * * **Task A (Medium):** Requires interpretive reasoning. The AI must move beyond surface-level summarization to infer intent, identify conflicting data points, or predict a singular outcome. It requires the AI to apply the persona’s "expert lens" to prioritize which data columns truly matter for a specific decision.
    * **Task B (High):** Requires multi-dimensional synthesis and adversarial reasoning. The AI must cross-reference disparate data sources to resolve systemic contradictions, simulate secondary effects of specific decisions, and formulate a high-stakes strategy. 

**Each Task Requirement must include:**
1. **Strategic Intent:** The mission-critical objective and professional stakes.
2. **Data Weighting:** Instructions on "ground truth" vs. "noise" and handling nulls.
3. **Execution Steps (CoT):** A step-by-step methodology for the AI.
4. **Tone & Style:** Vocabulary constraints and expert-to-expert nuances.
5. **Content Requirements:** Essential KPIs or arguments that must be present.
6. **Constraint Checklist:** "What NOT to do" (e.g., prohibited jargon, specific hallucinations).
7. **Evaluation Rubric:** 2–3 criteria for success.
8. **Difficulty Level:** Labeled clearly as "Medium" or "High".

    "abstract":"we compare the time evolution of entanglement measures after local operator excitation in the critical ising model with predictions from conformal field theory . for the spin operator and its descendants 
 we find that rnyi entropies of a block of spins increase by a constant that matches the logarithm of the quantum dimension of the conformal family . 
 however , for the energy operator we find a small constant contribution that differs from the conformal field theory answer equal to zero . 
 we argue that the mismatch is caused by the subtleties in the identification between the local operators in conformal field theory and their lattice counterpart . 
 our results indicate that evolution of entanglement measures in locally excited states not only constraints this identification , but also can be used to extract non - trivial data about the conformal field theory that governs the critical point . 
 we generalize our analysis to the ising model away from the critical point , states with multiple local excitations , as well as the evolution of the relative entropy after local operator excitation and discuss universal features that emerge from numerics .

    "abstract":"debris disks are thought to be sculptured by neighboring planets . 
 the same is true for the edgeworth - kuiper debris disk , yet no direct observational evidence for signatures of giant planets in the kuiper belt dust distribution has been found so far . 
 here we model the dust distribution in the outer solar system to reproduce the dust impact rates onto the dust detector onboard the new horizons spacecraft measured so far and to predict the rates during the neptune orbit traverse . to this end , we take a realistic distribution of transneptunian objects to launch a sufficient number of dust grains of different sizes and follow their orbits by including radiation pressure , poynting - robertson and stellar wind drag , as well as the perturbations of four giant planets . in a subsequent statistical analysis , we calculate number densities and lifetimes of the dust grains in order to simulate a collisional cascade . 
 in contrast to the previous work , our model not only considers collisional elimination of particles , but also includes production of finer debris . 
 we find that particles captured in the @xmath0:@xmath1 resonance with neptune build clumps that are not removed by collisions , because the depleting effect of collisions is counteracted by production of smaller fragments . 
 our model successfully reproduces the dust impact rates measured by new horizons out to @xmath2 and predicts an increase of the impact rate of about a factor of two or three around the neptune orbit crossing . 
 this result is robust with respect to the variation of the vaguely known number of dust - producing scattered disk objects , collisional outcomes , and the dust properties ."

    "article":"inflation offers a simple solution to the shortcomings of the standard hot big bang model . 
 in addition , its predictions about the initial density perturbations , leading to the observed structure formation , are in a remarkable agreement with measurements of the cosmic microwave background ( cmb ) temperature anisotropies . among the various inflationary models , 
 one should select the ones which lead to a better agreement with data , with the additional requirement that such models should be naturally built within a fundamental theoretical framework . in spite of its enormous success 
 , inflation remains still a paradigm in search of a model .    despite the elegance of chaotic inflation  @xcite 
 , this simple model faces a fine tuning problem . 
 consistency , between predictions for the amplitude of cmb temperature anisotropies and measurements , requires a tiny coupling constant . to avoid this problem , 
 linde  @xcite has proposed hybrid inflation , a model of inflation based on einstein gravity , but driven by a false vacuum . in this model , 
 the inflaton field rolls while another scalar field remains trapped in a false vacuum state . 
 the false vacuum becomes unstable when the magnitude of the inflaton field falls below some critical value , leading to a phase transition to the true vacuum . 
 the energy density is dominated by the false vacuum energy density so that the phase transition signals the end of hybrid inflation . 
 the phase transition at the end of inflation leads to topological defect formation  @xcite . 
 theoretically motivated inflationary models can be built in a context of supersymmetry ( susy ) and supergravity ( sugra ) theories . 
 @xmath1 supersymmetric models contain complex scalar fields , which often have flat directions in their potential , thus offering natural candidates for inflationary models . in this framework , hybrid inflation ( driven by the f - terms or the d - terms ) are the most standard models . 
 such inflationary models lead generically to cosmic string formation at the end of the inflationary era .

 d - term hybrid inflation is a successful and interesting model . in the context of supergravity 
 , d - term inflation avoids the _ hubble - induced mass _ problem , which plagues f - term hybrid inflation , while it can easily be implemented in string theory . in a standard formulation of d - term inflation , where the constant fi term gets compensated by a single complex scalar field , we do not add an additional discrete symmetry , and do not consider non - renormalisable terms in the potential , d - term strings are formed at the end of the phase transitions which signals the end of inflation . 
 these strings are analogous to the d - strings formed at the end of brane inflation , which is the result of brane collisions . 
 d - term inflation can not be studied in the standard formulation of supergravity , which is ill - defined whenever the superpotential vanishes and there are present constant fayet iliopoulos terms . following an effective supergravity formulation based on superconformal theory , the superpotential transforms under the u(1 ) symmetry along the directions where the fi terms are constant . 
 this transformation defines the charge assignments of the superfields . 
 d - term inflation has to be studied within this new formulation of supergravity , which is well defined when the superpotential vanishes . 
 cosmic strings contribute to the cosmic microwave background temperature anisotropies . 
 all current measurements put severe constraints on the allowed cosmic string contribution . to achieve a compatibility between measurements and theoretical predictions one 
 should fine tune the couplings . 
 this was already found in the case of minimal supergravity . 
 it was therefore natural to ask the question of whether this result still holds in non - minimal supergravity . 
 it was previously claimed in the literature that higher order khler potentials suppress the cosmic strings contribution . studying a case of non - minimal supergravity , where we include higher order corrections in the khler potential , as well as supergravity with shift symmetry 
 we conclude that cosmic string contribution will be dominant unless the couplings are fine - tuned .

 .  @xcite .    in conclusion 
 , we definitely disagree with the statement that non - minimal khler potentials avoid the cosmic strings problem , which should imply that fine tuning is not necessary . 
 even though we have not studied a large number of khler potentials , our current findings indicate that the problem of fine tuning is unavoidable unless one considers a more complicated model , for example where strings become topologically unstable , namely semi - local strings .

tasks_info.task_requirement:
**Strategic Intent:**
Your mission is to enable highly efficient, high-volume strategic technology forecasting. The user relies on no-code Business Intelligence (BI) dashboards to visualize emerging tech trends across millions of academic papers. However, the average 6,000-word length of these scientific articles makes full-text API processing prohibitively expensive and slow. Your task is to extract, interpret, and format the core commercial and technological signals using *only* the paper's highly compressed metadata, transforming dense academic prose into a structured, BI-ready schema.

**Data Weighting & Handling:**
- **Primary Ground Truth:** The `abstract` column. This is your definitive source for the core innovation.
- **Structural Context:** The `section_names` column. Use this to infer the empirical rigor of the paper (e.g., are there sections for "Experimental Setup" vs. just "Theoretical Proofs"?).
- **Noise/Exclusion:** Completely IGNORE the `article` column. If raw full-text is provided, disregard it to optimize latency and cognitive focus.
- **Handling Nulls:** If `section_names` are missing, default to "Rigor Unknown" in your output metrics.

**Execution Steps (Chain of Thought):**
1. **Abstract Parsing:** Scan the `abstract` to identify the specific STEM discipline and the primary technological innovation or thesis.
2. **Rigor Inference:** Cross-reference the innovation with the `section_names`. Deduce whether this is early-stage theory, computational simulation, or a physical applied experiment.
3. **TRL Estimation:** Based on steps 1 and 2, estimate the Technology Readiness Level (TRL 1-9).
4. **JSON Synthesis:** Map your findings into a strict, flat JSON structure suitable for immediate ingestion into a no-code BI database.

**Tone & Style:**
Maintain a highly objective, data-centric, and executive tone. Avoid academic fluff. Write as if you are populating a database for a C-suite technology forecaster. 

**Content Requirements:**
Your output must strictly be a JSON object containing the following keys: `core_innovation` (1 sentence), `stem_domain` (e.g., "Quantum Cryptography", "Astrophysics"), `inferred_trl` (integer 1-9), `evidence_of_rigor` (brief justification based on section names), and `commercial_viability_score` (1-10).

**Constraint Checklist:**

**Strategic Intent:** Your mission is to bridge the gap between dense, specialized academic research and the general public. You must translate a highly technical scientific paper into an engaging, accessible news brief without diluting the core scientific truth or introducing any hallucinations. This output will be used by science journalists to inform the public about new discoveries.

**Data Weighting:**
- **Ground Truth:** Treat the 'abstract' column as the absolute ground truth for the core claims and outcomes of the study. 
- **Narrative Context:** Use the 'article' column to extract real-world implications, analogies, and experimental context. 
- **Noise Reduction:** Treat all LaTeX mathematical notations (e.g., tokens starting with `@xmath`) as opaque variables. Do not attempt to solve, parse, or explicitly explain the math. Instead, abstract them as 'mathematical models', 'computational frameworks', or 'statistical thresholds'.

**Execution Steps (Chain-of-Thought):**
1. **Core Extraction:** Read the 'abstract' to identify the primary discovery, the problem being solved, and the final result.
2. **Contextual Scanning:** Scan the 'article' using the 'section_names' as a map (specifically looking for 'Introduction' and 'Conclusion' or 'Discussion') to find the real-world motivation and the practical applications of the research.
3. **De-Jargonization:** Translate the core extraction into layperson terms. Replace highly specialized terminology with intuitive analogies (e.g., comparing a 'convex billiard' chaotic system to predicting the erratic bounces of a pinball).
4. **Synthesis:** Draft a 3-part news brief: (a) The Headline, (b) The Breakdown (what they did), and (c) The Impact (why it matters to the world).

**Tone & Style:** 
Accessible, engaging, and authoritative. Write at the level of a high-quality publication like *Scientific American* or *Wired*. The tone should inspire curiosity but remain strictly objective.

**Content Requirements:**
- A punchy, non-clickbait headline.
- A 2-sentence executive summary.
- An 'Analogy/Metaphor' section that grounds the complex science in everyday concepts.
- A 'Real-World Impact' statement.

**Constraint Checklist:**
- DO NOT hallucinate dates, applications, or affiliations not explicitly stated in the text.
- DO NOT attempt to explain the `@xmath` variables; abstract them away.
- DO NOT use definitive words like 'proves' or 'cures' unless explicitly stated in the abstract; use 'suggests', 'demonstrates', or 'indicates'.
- DO NOT include dense academic jargon without an immediate, simple definition.

**Evaluation Rubric:**
1. **Translation Efficacy:** Does the summary make sense to a high school graduate without losing the scientific core?
2. **Factual Integrity:** Are all claims perfectly aligned with the 'abstract' without any extrapolation?
3. **Noise Handling:** Were all LaTeX tokens successfully bypassed without disrupting the narrative flow?

- **Risk Source:** The 'article' column (specifically 'Discussion', 'Limitations', or 'Methodology' sections identified via 'section_names') must be mined for experimental constraints, sample sizes, or limiting factors.
- **Noise Mitigation:** Mathematical proofs (`@xmath`) should be skipped for semantic meaning, but their presence should be noted as a structural indicator of 'theoretical/computational methodology' rather than empirical, physical testing.

**Execution Steps (Chain-of-Thought):**
1. **Scientific Consensus Mapping:** Read the 'abstract' and 'article' to establish exactly what was tested, what was observed, and what was merely hypothesized.
2. **Adversarial Persona Activation:** Put on the hat of a sensationalist journalist. How could the core finding be twisted into clickbait? (e.g., turning 'a theoretical model of quantum tricycles' into 'Scientists invent infinite quantum energy').
3. **Public Translation Draft:** Write a 2-paragraph public summary that is bulletproof against this sensationalism.
4. **Fact-Check & Mitigation Matrix:** Construct an audit table containing three columns: [Layperson Claim] | [Source Text Citation (Exact quote from 'article' or 'abstract')] | [Media Misinterpretation Risk & Clarification].

**Tone & Style:**
Clinical, highly rigorous, and extremely precise. The translation should be clear and accessible, while the audit matrix must be analytical and critical.

- A concise, precise public translation (max 200 words).
- A 'Sensationalism Risk' warning outlining the worst-case misinterpretation of the data.
- A 3-column 'Factual Integrity Matrix' explicitly linking at least 3 simplified claims back to their exact source text.
- An explicit 'What This Study DOES NOT Mean' bulleted list.

**Constraint Checklist:**
- DO NOT drop critical context regarding experimental limitations (e.g., if a study is theoretical, do not imply physical implementation).
- DO NOT attempt to validate the mathematical logic inside the LaTeX; validate the *verbal conclusions* drawn from it.
- DO NOT generate any claim in the public translation that cannot be directly mapped to the source text in the matrix.

**Evaluation Rubric:**
1. **Adversarial Rigor:** Does the AI successfully anticipate and neutralize likely media oversimplifications?
2. **Traceability:** Is every claim in the translation perfectly mapped to an exact, non-hallucinated quote from the source columns?
3. **Safety & Precision:** Does the output safely navigate around the LaTeX noise without losing the narrative thread of the scientific limitations?

tasks_info.task_name: Abstract Integrity and IMRAD Structural Audit
tasks_info.task_requirement:
### Strategic Intent
Your mission is to perform a rigorous editorial audit of an academic manuscript. You must verify that the highly compressed author-provided abstract is a faithful, non-exaggerated representation of the dense 6,000-word body text. You will evaluate the abstract's adherence to the standard IMRAD (Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion) structure, ensuring the journal's standards for transparency and academic integrity are upheld without requiring the auditor to manually read the entire text.

### Data Weighting
* **`abstract`**: The Target. This is the text you are auditing for compliance and accuracy.
* **`article`**: The Ground Truth. All claims in the abstract must be firmly anchored here.
* **`section_names`**: The Roadmap. Use these headers to navigate the logical flow of the article.
* **Noise Handling**: Treat all `@xmath` and `@xcite` tokens as standard mathematical formulas and citations. Do not attempt to decode them; simply read around them to extract the semantic meaning of the surrounding text.

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Structural Mapping (IMRAD)**: Analyze the `abstract` and categorize its sentences into Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion. Cross-reference this flow against the `section_names` to ensure structural alignment.
2. **Claim Extraction**: Isolate the 3-5 core scientific claims, findings, or metrics presented in the `abstract`.
3. **Fidelity Verification**: For each extracted claim, scan the `article` (using `section_names` as a guide) to locate the corresponding source text.
4. **Exaggeration Analysis**: Compare the tone and absoluteness of the abstract's claims against the nuances of the article. Look for "spin"—where a highly caveated result in the article is presented as a definitive breakthrough in the abstract.
5. **Audit Report Generation**: Compile your findings into a structured editorial QA report.

### Tone & Style
Maintain an objective, rigorous, and professional editorial tone. Write as a Senior Managing Editor addressing a peer. Be precise and definitive. Avoid technical machine-learning jargon.

### Content Requirements
* An **IMRAD Completeness Score** (Pass/Partial/Fail) with a brief justification.
* A **Claim Verification Table** listing each abstract claim, the corresponding article evidence, and a status (Verified, Exaggerated, Unsupported).
* A brief **Editorial Verdict** summarizing the abstract's fidelity and readiness for publication.

### Constraint Checklist
* DO NOT use NLP evaluation metrics like ROUGE, BLEU, or BERTScore. 
* DO NOT hallucinate formulas or decode `@xmath`/`@xcite` tokens.
* DO NOT summarize the paper; you are auditing the existing summary.
* DO NOT recommend rejection based on the science itself, only on the fidelity of the summary.

### Evaluation Rubric
1. **Traceability**: Every claim analyzed from the abstract must be explicitly linked to a specific section/concept in the source article.
2. **Nuance Detection**: Successfully identifies subtle exaggerations or omissions between the compressed abstract and the dense article.
3. **Editorial Usability**: The final output is immediately actionable for a QA auditor with zero coding or NLP background.
tasks_info.elevator_pitch_summary: Automates the tedious QA process of checking if a 150-word abstract exaggerates the 6,000-word main paper, saving editors hours of manual reading and reducing human error.
tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: The breakthrough here is bypassing traditional, mathematical NLP metrics like ROUGE, which our persona inherently distrusts and misunderstands. Instead, we use a semantic IMRAD-based Chain of Thought extraction. The AI maps abstract claims directly to the body text, deliberately ignoring LaTeX noise (`@xmath`) to focus purely on semantic fidelity. It determines whether the author over-promised their results in the abstract, providing a highly legible, "editor-to-editor" audit report that directly solves the persona's workflow friction.

tasks_info.task_name: Adversarial Risk Assessment & Editorial Strategy Formulation
tasks_info.task_requirement:
### Strategic Intent
Your objective is to act as a rigorous, adversarial Senior Quality Assurance Editor protecting the journal's reputation. You must synthesize the dense `article` to uncover methodological caveats, boundary conditions, or systemic uncertainties that the authors have obscured or entirely omitted in their highly compressed `abstract`. You will simulate the secondary effects of publishing the paper as-is (e.g., peer backlash, reproducibility failures) and formulate a high-stakes editorial strategy to enforce absolute transparency.

### Data Weighting
* **`article`**: The Primary Target. Hunt specifically for sections discussing limitations, noise, edge cases, and methodological assumptions.
* **`abstract`**: The Baseline. Evaluate this for what is *missing* rather than what is present.
* **`section_names`**: The Contextual Map. Use this to locate "Discussion", "Conclusion", or "Limitations" sections quickly.
* **Noise Handling**: Navigate fluidly around `@xmath` and `@xcite` tokens. Focus on the transitional phrasing (e.g., "However, we assume...", "This breaks down when...") rather than the mathematical proofs themselves.

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Deconstruct Methodological Assumptions**: Deep-scan the `article` for caveats, error margins, unproven assumptions, or explicitly stated limitations by the authors.
2. **Adversarial Cross-Reference**: Compare these discovered limitations against the `abstract`. Identify "sins of omission"—critical context that was stripped away during the 40x compression process, resulting in a misleadingly confident summary.
3. **Secondary Effect Simulation**: Predict the specific academic risks if this paper is published with its current abstract. (e.g., Will industry practitioners misapply the mathematical model? Will peer reviewers attack the lack of transparency?)
4. **Strategy Formulation**: Draft a mandatory "Revise & Resubmit" (R&R) directive for the authors, outlining exactly how the abstract must be rewritten to reflect the underlying systemic realities of the research.

### Tone & Style
Authoritative, critical, risk-aware, and uncompromising. Use the vocabulary of senior academic publishing (e.g., "methodological transparency," "reproducibility risk," "epistemological overreach").

### Content Requirements
* An **Omission Ledger**: A detailed list of critical limitations present in the article but missing from the abstract.
* A **Risk Impact Matrix**: An assessment of the reputational and scientific risks of publishing the current abstract (Low/Medium/High).
* **Mandatory Revision Directives**: 2-3 specific, actionable demands for the authors to rewrite their abstract.

### Constraint Checklist
* DO NOT evaluate the mathematical accuracy of the formulas (you are an editor, not a peer reviewer for the specific domain).
* DO NOT suggest computational/NLP fixes (e.g., "tune the LLM"); keep solutions entirely within the realm of editorial workflows.
* DO NOT use generic advice; references to omissions must be hyper-specific to the text provided.

### Evaluation Rubric
1. **Adversarial Depth**: Successfully unearths hidden contradictions or buried caveats in the 6,000-word text that surface-level summarization misses.
2. **Impact Simulation**: Provides highly realistic, academically grounded consequences for publishing misleading abstracts.
3. **Strategic Actionability**: The revision directives are firm, clear, and ready to be copy-pasted into an author correspondence email.

The prompt forces the AI to hunt for systemic contradictions and "sins of omission" between the highly compressed abstract and the dense article. It simulates the exact mindset of a veteran QA editor looking for hidden risks. By outputting a risk matrix and an author revision plan, it transforms raw, math-heavy text into a high-stakes editorial decision engine, perfectly aligning with the persona's goal of ensuring auditability and transparency.

task_1.judgement: The synthesized task is tightly aligned with the arXiv long-form summarization dataset: it audits the author-written abstract (target) against the full article (source) using section headers as a navigation aid. task_1.improvement_suggestion: Add a section-normalization layer that maps common arXiv headers to IMRAD equivalents (e.g., Background/Related Work -> Introduction, Experiments -> Methods/Results, Analysis -> Results/Discussion, Conclusion -> Discussion) and require per-claim evidence capture with section name + paragraph index + a short verbatim quote. Include an explicit ‘Caveat Delta’ field for each claim to log hedging/limitations present in the article but absent in the abstract. task_2.judgement: Strong, domain-faithful alignment. The persona’s editorial QA focus directly leverages the dataset’s article–abstract pairing and section headers to surface omissions under high compression. The task is feasible and high-stakes without external tools, respects zero-coding constraints, and explicitly accounts for arXiv-specific noise (LaTeX tokens, long-range dependencies). tasks_info.task_name: Section-Guided Skim Mapping & Token Optimization Strategy
tasks_info.task_requirement:
## Strategic Intent
As a UX/Product Strategist relying on AI playgrounds, your goal is to design a prompt sequence that circumvents the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon without inflating backend token costs. You will analyze the provided `abstract` and `section_names` to create a 'Student Reading Guide'. This guide will instruct the AI copilot on exactly *which* sections of the 6,000-word `article` to target for specific scientific concepts, eliminating the need to process the entire document at once.

## Data Weighting
* **Ground Truth:** Treat the `abstract` as the core summary of intent.
* **Structural Map:** Use `section_names` (if available, or infer them from the text's natural transitions) to map the document.
* **Noise Filter:** Ignore the dense `article` body for now; focus strictly on mapping the abstract's claims to hypothetical text sections.

## Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Deconstruct the Abstract:** Break down the `abstract` into 3-4 core scientific claims or objectives.
2. **Structural Mapping:** Hypothesize which specific sections of a standard academic paper (e.g., Introduction, Methodology, Results, Discussion) would house the detailed evidence for each claim.
3. **Token-Optimized Prompt Strategy:** Draft a system prompt for the copilot that instructs it to sequentially extract data *only* from these targeted sections based on the student's current question.
4. **UX Output Generation:** Design the user-facing UI copy for a 'Smart Skim Path', showing the student exactly which sections they should read to understand the abstract's claims.

## Tone & Style
Instructional, UX-focused, and highly structured. Use the tone of a senior product designer outlining a feature flow to a UI team.

## Content Requirements
* A numbered breakdown of the abstract's core claims.
* A mapped 'Skim Path' connecting claims to paper sections.
* A draft System Prompt for the AI copilot to execute this selective reading strategy.

## Constraint Checklist
* **DO NOT** write API calls, Python scripts, or backend integration code.
* **DO NOT** instruct the AI to summarize the entire 6,000-word article at once.

tasks_info.task_requirement:
## Strategic Intent
Standard LLMs often drop critical scientific nuances buried in the middle of long texts, outputting summaries that closely mirror the `abstract` but miss the actual discoveries. As a Product Strategist, you must red-team the AI's capability. You will hunt for a crucial 'middle-text delta'—a vital finding or limitation in the `article` body that is entirely absent from the `abstract`. You will then translate this highly technical, noisy text into an accessible, trustworthy 'Deep Dive Alert' UX feature for a university student.

## Data Weighting
* **Primary Ground Truth:** The middle 50% of the `article` (usually Results/Discussion).
* **Adversarial Baseline:** The `abstract` (representing what a naive AI summarization would output).
* **Noise Mitigation:** The text contains heavy tokenization artifacts (e.g., `ly@xmath0`, `[ feii ]`, uncased text, citation brackets). These must be aggressively filtered out.

## Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Delta Identification:** Scan the deep body of the `article`. Identify one highly specific scientific finding, anomaly, or limitation that is *not* mentioned in the `abstract`.
2. **The 'Aha!' Synthesis:** Explain why missing this specific detail would harm a student's understanding of the paper.
3. **Noise Neutralization:** Translate the raw text surrounding this finding. Convert the broken LaTeX (e.g., `@xmath` variables) and citation noise into readable, context-aware English.
4. **UX Copywriting:** Draft the UI text for a 'Copilot Deep Dive Alert'. This is a pop-up or side-panel module that says, "Wait, standard summaries missed this crucial detail..." and presents your clean translation.

## Tone & Style
Critically evaluative in the analysis phase; empathetic, engaging, and highly polished in the UX copywriting phase.

## Content Requirements
* Quote the specific 'lost' raw text from the middle of the article.
* A comparative analysis showing why the abstract failed to capture this.
* The fully cleaned, plain-English translation of the finding.
* The exact UI copy for the 'Deep Dive Alert' module.

## Constraint Checklist
* **DO NOT** output any raw `@xmath` or formatting tags in the final UI copy.
* **DO NOT** hallucinate findings; the extracted delta must exist in the provided `article`.
* **DO NOT** propose backend engineering fixes (e.g., "implement sparse attention"). Solve this purely through prompt synthesis and UX presentation.

## Evaluation Rubric
1. **Adversarial Success:** Did the AI successfully locate a meaningful discrepancy between the article body and the abstract?
2. **Translation Quality:** Is the scientific noise (LaTeX/artifacts) accurately converted into legible academic concepts?
3. **UX Efficacy:** Does the 'Deep Dive Alert' build trust with the student user?
tasks_info.elevator_pitch_summary: Force the AI to find a crucial insight buried in the middle of the article that the abstract missed, then translate the dense LaTeX noise into a student-friendly UX alert.
tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: This is a rigorous adversarial stress-test designed for a prompt engineer/UX persona. It tackles both the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon and the formatting degradation inherent in arXiv datasets. By forcing the AI to manually locate a 'middle-text delta' and scrub the text of `@xmath` tokenization noise, the task proves the AI's value beyond simple abstract-regurgitation. It transforms raw, hostile data into a trust-building product feature ('Deep Dive Alert') relying entirely on high-order cognitive synthesis and UX framing, completely bypassing the need for backend code.

task_1.judgement: Strong alignment: The persona’s UX/prompt-design remit directly exploits the dataset’s abstract and section_names to build a selective-reading strategy that addresses long-context failure modes and token costs. The task is feasible within the schema (no external tools/code) and is practically meaningful for a student-facing research copilot. It requires nontrivial reasoning to decompose abstract claims, map them to canonical sections, and design a token-aware prompt flow. Minor gaps: variability in arXiv section naming (e.g., Preliminaries, Related Work, Background, Appendix) and cross-domain styles are not explicitly handled; concrete token budgets, fallback routing when section_names are sparse/missing, and paragraph-level targeting rules could be made more explicit. Overall, this is a well-scoped, high-utility task tightly grounded in the dataset.
task_1.improvement_suggestion: Add a concrete, schema-native routing protocol: (1) Normalize section_names to a canonical set (Introduction, Background/Preliminaries, Methods, Results, Discussion/Conclusion, Limitations, Appendix), with synonyms and regex fallbacks; (2) For each abstract claim, generate 3–5 keyphrases and map them to top-2 candidate sections; (3) Enforce a paragraph-level budget (e.g., read only the first/last two paragraphs of each target section plus any figure/table captions encountered) to cap tokens; (4) Include a no-section fallback that scans only headers and the first sentence after each header to locate likely evidence; (5) Add guardrails to mask equations/citations in the student UI while preserving them for internal retrieval; (6) Define a light A/B rubric (tokens consumed, answer accuracy vs. gold abstract, time-to-answer) for UX validation in playgrounds. This preserves zero-coding constraints while improving robustness across diverse arXiv formats.

(2) Noise-normalization checklist: strip inline citations [#], LaTeX math, figure/table callouts; replace @xmathN with the nearest-defined symbol name or a neutral placeholder (e.g., “the parameter”) if undefined; standardize chemical/ion tags (e.g., Fe II) and units. (3) Delta verification step: list three distinctive technical terms from the quoted passage that do not appear verbatim in the abstract to justify absence without external tools. (4) UX copy constraints: cap at 120 words, include the originating section name for provenance, and forbid any raw math tokens. (5) Replace chain-of-thought exposure with concise bullet rationales to maintain clarity while avoiding unnecessary reasoning transcripts.

tasks_info.task_requirement:
### Strategic Intent
Your objective is to act as a forensic IP technical screener. Your primary mission is to identify specific, enabling technical disclosures (prior art) buried within highly complex academic text that could invalidate competitor patent claims. You are serving an expert patent strategist who cannot write code or query databases, but whose career depends on absolute factual precision. A single missed detail (like a specific mathematical variable, algorithm constraint, or chemical compound) could result in millions of dollars in legal liability.

### Data Weighting
- **Ground Truth:** The `article` field is your absolute source of truth. 
- **Contextual Framing:** Use the `abstract` strictly to understand the high-level intent of the research, but *never* rely on it for technical extraction.
- **Noise Handling:** The text contains heavy LaTeX formatting, citation markers (e.g., `@xcite`), and mathematical notation (e.g., `@xmath`). Do not let this disrupt your parsing. Translate mathematical relationships into precise plain-English technical descriptions where possible, or preserve them exactly as stated if translation risks altering the meaning.

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Abstract Baseline:** Briefly analyze the `abstract` to define the paper's core scientific domain and overarching claim.
2. **Deep Methodological Scan:** Traverse the 6,000+ word `article` specifically hunting for "how-to" elements: algorithms, formulas, material properties, and experimental setups. Ignore literature reviews and philosophical discussions.
3. **Isolate & Extract:** Identify 2-3 highly specific technical mechanisms buried in the text that are *not* mentioned in the abstract. Extract the exact quotes and their surrounding context.
4. **Legal Viability Assessment:** For each extracted mechanism, assess its viability as "prior art" based on three criteria: 
   - *Specificity:* Is the mechanism detailed enough to be reproduced?
   - *Novelty Indicator:* Does the text present this as a novel contribution or a known baseline?
   - *Claim Mapping:* What type of patent claim might this invalidate (e.g., a software method claim, a system architecture claim)?

### Tone & Style
Objective, legally rigorous, and highly analytical. Use precise patent-law terminology (e.g., "enabling disclosure," "methodology," "prior art mapping") while avoiding all software development jargon (e.g., "parsing strings," "API calls," "regex matching").

### Content Requirements
- **Domain Summary:** A 2-sentence overview of the technology.
- **Buried Prior Art Discoveries:** At least 2 distinct technical methodologies or algorithms extracted from the `article` (complete with verbatim quote snippets).
- **Prior Art Viability Matrix:** A breakdown of each discovery's specificity and potential target claim type.

### Constraint Checklist
- DO NOT summarize the entire paper; focus only on actionable technical mechanisms.
- DO NOT hallucinate or infer capabilities the authors did not explicitly state.
- DO NOT output code, JSON, or command-line instructions. The output must be a readable, executive-level legal briefing.
- DO NOT rely on the abstract for the Prior Art Discoveries.

### Evaluation Rubric
1. **Extraction Fidelity:** Did the AI successfully bypass the abstract to find buried, granular technical truths in the article?
2. **Persona Alignment:** Is the output immediately usable by a non-technical patent lawyer for legal strategy, free of programming jargon?
tasks_info.elevator_pitch_summary: The AI acts as a forensic paralegal, bypassing high-level summaries to extract buried algorithmic and mathematical details from dense academic text to serve as patent-invalidating prior art.
tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: This task addresses the persona's core workflow friction: critical IP details are often lost in the 40:1 compression ratio of scientific abstracts. By instructing the AI to treat the `abstract` merely as a primer and forcing a deep scan of the `article` for 'enabling disclosures,' we bridge the gap between noisy LaTeX datasets and high-stakes legal utility. The AI handles the semantic parsing of math and citations, outputting a precise triage document that a patent lawyer can use immediately without needing any underlying data schema knowledge.

tasks_info.task_requirement:
### Strategic Intent
Your objective is to conduct an adversarial IP teardown. You must evaluate a highly technical scientific paper to identify structural contradictions, unproven assumptions, or explicitly stated limitations buried within the methodology or discussion sections. You will use these buried vulnerabilities to simulate how a competitor might "design around" a hypothetical patent based on this research. The end-user is an advanced risk-mitigation strategist who requires audit-level factual precision to protect internal intellectual property.

### Data Weighting
- **Contradiction Mapping:** Contrast the sweeping claims made in the `abstract` against the granular constraints, edge cases, and error rates detailed in the late stages of the `article`.
- **Structural Cues:** Leverage `section_names` (if available) or implicit structural transitions (e.g., "However, some of these features...", "Caveats exist...") to locate methodological weaknesses.
- **Noise Handling:** Carefully decode LaTeX noise specifically when it relates to boundary conditions, thresholds, or mathematical limits, as these are prime targets for patent design-arounds.

### Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)
1. **Claim vs. Reality Audit:** Read the `abstract` to identify the "idealized" invention. Then, scan the `article` (especially methodologies, results, and discussion) for caveats, boundary conditions, or failed test cases.
2. **Vulnerability Extraction:** Pinpoint exact quotes that demonstrate a limitation of the proposed technology (e.g., "the algorithm fails when X > Y", "we assumed equal-size impactors"). 
3. **Adversarial Design-Around Simulation:** Adopting the mindset of a competitor, propose a technical workaround that exploits the extracted limitations. How could a competitor achieve a similar result by operating just outside the stated mathematical or physical boundaries of this paper?
4. **Risk Mitigation Strategy:** Formulate a proactive legal strategy for the persona. Should they file a broader continuation patent covering the edge cases? Should they publish defensive prior art to block the competitor's design-around?

### Tone & Style
Adversarial, deeply critical, and strategically forward-looking. The language must be authoritative and suitable for a boardroom presentation on corporate IP risk. 

### Content Requirements
- **The Delta Analysis:** A direct comparison between the abstract's promises and the article's buried realities.
- **Vulnerability Log:** 2-3 specific technical limitations extracted verbatim from the text.
- **Competitor Exploitation Scenario:** A step-by-step narrative of how a rival could legally bypass the technology based on the vulnerabilities.
- **Defensive Action Plan:** Concrete IP strategy recommendations (e.g., patent claim broadening, defensive publishing).

### Constraint Checklist
- DO NOT present the paper's findings at face value; you must interrogate its weaknesses.
- DO NOT provide general business advice; confine the strategy strictly to IP, patents, and technical boundaries.
- DO NOT fail to cite the specific text (including mathematical boundaries if applicable) that justifies the vulnerability.
- DO NOT suggest any software or scripting tools to the user.

### Evaluation Rubric
1. **Adversarial Synthesis:** Did the AI successfully identify the delta between the abstract's high-level claims and the article's nuanced limitations?
2. **Strategic Translation:** Is the design-around simulation physically/mathematically logical based on the text, and is the resulting mitigation strategy actionable for a patent lawyer?
tasks_info.elevator_pitch_summary: The AI performs an adversarial teardown of a scientific paper, finding buried limitations and edge cases to simulate how a competitor might legally bypass a patent based on this research.
tasks_info.deep_dive_summary: This task pushes the AI to perform complex multi-dimensional synthesis. It requires the AI to read the text adversarially—looking for the 'delta' between the high-level abstract claims and the deep-in-the-weeds caveats of the article. By forcing the AI to identify boundary conditions (often hidden in LaTeX math notation) and simulate a 'design-around' strategy, we transform raw, noisy academic data into a high-value corporate risk mitigation playbook. It perfectly aligns with the persona's need for advanced IP strategy while entirely abstracting away the data engineering layer.

task_1.judgement: The task is strongly aligned with the arXiv article–abstract schema: it leverages the full article as the enabling source for granular technical disclosures and uses the abstract solely for topical orientation, matching the dataset’s long-input/short-summary structure. It is feasible without external tools and respects the persona’s zero-coding constraint by prescribing a readable legal briefing with targeted extractions. The task is materially significant for high-stakes prior-art screening and explicitly anticipates dataset noise (LaTeX, citations), directing precise plain-English restatements or faithful transcription. Minor gaps remain: the spec does not mandate firm citation anchors (section/paragraph/equation IDs) or publication/version dates needed for legal provenance, and it assumes the model can reliably traverse 6,000+ words without a defined chunking protocol; also, the “Chain of Thought” label is unnecessary and could be reframed to avoid process disclosure. Overall, this is a high-fidelity, well-calibrated task with small but addressable improvements for legal rigor and reproducibility.
task_1.improvement_suggestion: Add a mandatory Evidence & Citation Annex: for each extracted mechanism, include (a) section_names path and paragraph index; (b) equation/figure labels with exact LaTeX where applicable; (c) parameter definitions, units, boundary conditions, and experimental setup details; (d) two-sentence surrounding context; and (e) earliest available publication/arXiv version date—while renaming “Execution Steps (Chain of Thought)” to “Execution Steps” and requiring a brief reasoning summary—to ensure legally citable, reproducible, and time-stamped prior-art mapping within the dataset’s structure.

task_2.judgement: Strong alignment: the persona’s value-creation (IP risk and prior-art precision) directly leverages the dataset’s article vs abstract pairing, enabling contradiction mapping and limitation extraction. The task is executable using only the schema (article, abstract, section_names) and is highly meaningful for patent strategy. It respects the zero-coding constraint and demands adversarial, multi-layer reasoning. Minor caveat: the dataset lacks native location anchors (page/line IDs) and equation normalization, which can impede exact citation traceability and reproducibility when LaTeX noise is heavy or section_names is missing.
task_2.improvement_suggestion: Add a mandatory, auditable extraction protocol tied to the schema: for each quoted vulnerability, require (a) nearest section title from section_names, (b) a short unique n-gram anchor from the article to ensure verifiable retrieval, (c) the boundary condition rewritten in a normalized inequality form alongside the original LaTeX, and (d) a structured Delta table mapping abstract claims to specific method/result caveats. This improves traceability under LaTeX noise and ensures the design-around is mathematically referenced to in-text limits without extra tools.
